    Label Maker

    GHS Revision 7 chemical labels for Australian workplaces, sized for Avery label sheets. Hazard data comes from Safe Work Australia's HCIS where they list the chemical.

        0 selected
        Stock
          Reads the hazard section out of a supplier's sheet. PDF, Word .docx, and plain text or HTML (.txt, .md, .csv, .htm) can be read. Pictures cannot — .jpg, .png, .gif and scanned PDFs are images of words rather than words, and pulling text out of those needs OCR this page does not carry. Ask the supplier for the PDF, or copy the text and paste it.
          Find your chemical there, select the whole page (Ctrl+A), copy it (Ctrl+C), and paste it below. HCIS will not let a web page fetch it directly, so this is the way in — everything is read from what you paste, nothing is fetched.

          A Chemwatch record works here too, and is worth using where HCIS has no entry. Chemwatch classifies chemicals itself rather than waiting for someone to notify one, so it is usually fuller: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane has a single notification of H225 in the free registers, and seven statements in Chemwatch. It also gives the precautionary statements outright, which HCIS does not.
          Bromine water, limewater, Fehling's and the rest are mixtures, so PubChem has no record of them — a search either finds nothing or finds the pure chemical, whose classification is not theirs.
          For anything made up from more than one chemical — “copper sulfate 2.5% in 0.5 M sulfuric acid”, “bromine 5% in carbon tetrachloride”. No database holds a record for those, because a database indexes substances and a mixture is not one. Look each ingredient up, give its percentage, and the classification is worked out from them at the GHS cut-off concentrations — which is the part that matters: 0.5 M sulfuric acid is an irritant, not a corrosive, so copying the concentrated acid’s pictograms would over-warn.
          Classification comes from Safe Work Australia's HCIS where they list the chemical. Whatever is used, it is reported below after a lookup — always check it against the supplier's SDS.
          What was changed on this label

          Heading
          Kept for the record and for the QR code. The name printed on the label should be the one on the supplier's SDS, so a systematic name normally belongs here rather than in the Name field.
          Digits after a symbol drop automatically as subscripts; a trailing + or - rises as a charge. Use ^ or _ to force it (SO4^2-).
          Identifiers
          Tick this only when you know it has been classified and found to have no hazards — a supplier's sheet saying so, or HCIS holding no classification for it. The label then prints NON-HAZARDOUS instead of NO CLASSIFICATION FOUND. Leave it clear when you simply have not found a classification: those are different things, and only one of them is safe to print on a bottle. Ignored while the label carries hazard codes.
          Carries the name, formula, CAS, signal word, hazard codes, DG class, where to store it and what to keep it away from. Only added when the label is at least 80 × 50 mm — smaller than that a code cannot be printed large enough to scan reliably, so it is left off rather than shrunk.
          What changes at each strength
          Mixture — work the classification out from what went in

          For a solution of one chemical in another — “bromine solution 5% in carbon tetrachloride” — there is no compound record to look up, because the mixture is not a compound. Name what is in it and how much, and the classification is worked out from the components using the same cut-offs the Hazards step uses for a dilution.

          Pictograms
          Drag a pictogram down to add it, sideways to reorder, or back up to remove it. Tap also works.
          Available
          On this label
          Hazard statements
          GHS 7, including the Australian AUH additions.
          Precautionary statements
          Required on supplied (original) containers.
          Goes at the bottom of the label. Filled with today's date on a new label; change it to the date the bottle was actually filled. A shelf life or an expiry date means nothing without it.
          Minimum PPE
          Storage and use
          Storage compatibility
          Label options
          RiskAssess carries this as its “Users” field. A chemical prohibited under WHS Schedule 10 is detected from its CAS number and printed whatever is chosen here.
          Contents and preparation
          Transport and border
          The class says what kind of danger; the packing group says how much of it. A label with a class and no packing group is half a transport classification.
          Supplier details (required on original containers)
          These print on lab-tech bottles of pure chemicals. Fetching a chemical fills in whatever PubChem has; trim the values so they fit.
          Solubility codes
          Put this same HTML file on a web address staff and students can reach, and paste that address here. The chemical's details travel inside the QR code itself, so nothing is uploaded and no database is needed — the page just reads them back. Without a reachable address no QR code can be printed, because there would be nothing for a scan to open.
          A QR code supplements the printed label, it never replaces it. The GHS elements — product name, signal word, hazard statements and pictograms — have to be readable on the container itself. Use the code for the detail that will not fit.
          Where to publish this file so scans work on every phone

          You publish one file — this one — and never touch it again as you add chemicals. Each chemical's details ride inside its own QR code, so the hosted page holds no chemical data and needs no updating.

          Free options that work:

          • Netlify Drop — drag the file onto app.netlify.com/drop. No account needed to start. Fastest way to test one code before committing to anything.
          • GitHub Pages — free and permanent, needs a GitHub account. Good if this will be in use for years.
          • Cloudflare Pages — same idea, drag-and-drop deploy.
          • Your own school or department web space — best of all if you can get it, because the domain is already trusted by the school's web filter.

          What will not work, and why:

          • Teams / SharePoint / OneDrive — two separate blockers. Viewers are sent to a login, and SharePoint serves .html files with a download header instead of rendering them, which is the default and can no longer be switched off in most tenants.
          • Google Drive and Dropbox — both withdrew HTML page hosting years ago; shared links download the file.
          • A file on this computer — a phone cannot reach it, and camera apps ignore file:// links.

          Before printing a batch, scan one test code on a school-managed device, not just your own phone. Web filtering may block an unfamiliar domain, and getting one address allowlisted is a much smaller ask than a server.

          Safety card files

          Each card is one self-contained HTML file — artwork and text baked in, no internet, nothing to install. Put them on a shared drive or a USB stick and they open on any computer, tablet or phone. They are not what a QR code can point at, though: a phone scanning a code has to reach the page over the web, and cannot open a file sitting on someone else's computer.
          Sheets you have uploaded
          Searches the whole text, not just the name — so “carcinogen”, “H350” or “eyewash” all find sheets that mention them.

          What this program is
          
  
          It makes GHS Revision 7 workplace labels for chemicals
     decanted or stored in a prep room, and a one-page Mini SDS to go with
     them. It classifies from published data, it shows its working, and it
     does not replace a safety data sheet.
          

  
          
    Read this first. Every classification here is a draft
    until somebody checks it against the supplier's SDS for the container
    in front of them. The program is explicit about which source each
    answer came from precisely so that check is possible.
  
          

  
          How you make one
          
  
            
    
          1. Look up the chemical on the Chemical tab — type a
        name, CAS number or PubChem CID. The name, formula, hazard
        statements and pictograms fill in automatically.
            2. 
    
          2. Set the concentration, then press Apply
        concentration cut-offs on the Hazards tab. A dilute solution
        is often classified lower than the concentrated chemical, or not
        at all.
            3. 
    
          3. Check everything against the supplier's SDS and
        edit anything that looks wrong — every field stays editable.
            4. 
    
          4. Queue and print. Add labels to the print queue,
        or fill a whole page with one chemical, then preview the sheet
        before printing.
            5. 
  
          
  
          Nothing here replaces the SDS. Treat every fetched label
     as a first draft.
          

  
          How a label is built
          
  
          
    
    
          Steps 2 to 4 are automatic and reversible; every
      field stays editable afterwards, and an edited field is never
      re-derived behind you.
          
  
          

  
          Where the data comes from
          
  
          
    
          SourceUsed forHow it arrives
          
    
          
      HCIS
      The Australian regulatory classification, published concentration
          limits and workplace exposure standards.
      Pasted. HCIS sends no cross-origin header, so a
          browser refuses the request before it leaves this machine. The
          panel opens it in a tab and reads what you paste back.
    
          
    
          
      PubChem
      Names, formulae, physical properties, and a classification where
          HCIS has none.
      Fetched from its public API. Where PubChem
          mirrors a Safe Work Australia entry that entry is used alone;
          otherwise it pools international sources and the label says so.
    
          
    
          
      Supplier SDS
      Anything the two registers disagree on, and mixtures sold as a
          product.
      By hand. Test data on the actual mixture outranks
          any calculation — national guide, section 3.2.
    
          
    
          
      ADG Code
      Transport class, UN number, packing group and segregation.
      A local copy of the dangerous goods list. Appendix C emergency
          action codes are not included — they are
          licensed and may not be reproduced.
    
          
  
          
  
          Nothing is sent anywhere. The only outbound request this
     page makes is to PubChem, and only when you ask it to look something
     up.
          

  
          Which register to search, and why it matters
          
  
          Two registers, and they answer different questions. The choice sits
     beside the search box on the Chemical tab.
          
  
          
    
          PubChem
          
    
          International, and the only one this page can fetch directly.
        Search by name, CAS number or CID. Where Safe Work Australia has
        an entry that PubChem mirrors, that entry is used on its own and
        the label says so. Where it does not, PubChem pools every other
        source — EU, Japan, supplier sheets — and averages them, which is
        not the Australian classification and is flagged as such.
        Search on the CAS number where you have one.
        PubChem's name search matches words, not substances, and it fails
        quietly: searching “xylene” returns a corrosive amine,
        not the solvent.
          
    
          HCIS
          
    
          Safe Work Australia's own register, and the Australian regulatory
        classification. It cannot be fetched — HCIS sends no
        cross-origin header, so the browser refuses the request before it
        leaves this machine. Instead the panel opens HCIS in a new tab,
        and you paste the page back in; codes, pictograms, signal word,
        cut-off concentrations and exposure limits are read from what you
        paste. Worth doing for anything hazardous: PubChem does not carry
        every HCIS entry, and where it misses one it silently falls back
        to pooled data. Chromium trioxide returns twelve statements from
        HCIS and twenty-two from PubChem, disagreeing on which.
          
    
          Neither has it
          
    
          Common for dyes and stains. The label says no classification
        found, which is not the same as non-hazardous and is
        deliberately not written as though it were. Where a sheet has
        actually classified the chemical and found no hazards, tick
        This chemical is not hazardous on the Hazards tab and the
        label says non-hazardous instead.
          
  
          

  
          How the formula is worked out
          
  
          PubChem returns Hill notation: carbon first, then hydrogen, then
     everything else alphabetically — and for a compound with no carbon,
     strictly alphabetical. That is correct and unhelpful. It gives
     phosphorus pentoxide as O10P4 and sodium sulfate as Na2O4S.
          
  
          Every formula, however it arrives, goes through the same four steps,
     and the first one that has an answer wins:
          
  
            
    
          1. A hand-checked entry for that PubChem record.
        Needed where the answer depends on structure rather than
        composition — C2H6O is ethanol or dimethyl ether, and only a
        person can say which.
            2. 
    
          2. PubChem's own conventional formula, as its
        depositors wrote it. Checked to contain exactly the atoms the
        Hill formula does before it is accepted, so a typo in somebody
        else's record cannot reach your label.
            3. 
    
          3. The hydrate rebuild. The water count comes out
        of the name — “hexahydrate” is six — and is put back
        where it belongs: H12N2O12Zn becomes Zn(NO3)2·6H2O.
        Refused whenever the subtraction does not come out exactly,
        because a name and a formula that disagree mean one of them is
        wrong.
            4. 
    
          4. The element ordering sequence, which is the one
        IUPAC gives for the purpose. Metals lead; among the non-metals,
        hydrogen sits between the group 15 elements and the chalcogens,
        which is what makes NH3, PH3, H2O, H2S and HCl all come out
        right from a single rule.
            5. 
  
          
  
          This runs on a fresh lookup, on a pasted HCIS entry, on
     a version refresh, and on every label in an imported file.
     An import used to copy whatever the file said, so a library could be
     right and an import of it wrong. The import message now says how many
     formulas it rewrote, and each label's working records its own.
          
  
          Organic compounds are left in Hill order on purpose —
     for those it is the conventional molecular formula, and
     C6H12O6 is right as it stands. So are oxoacids, which write hydrogen
     first whatever the sequence says: HNO3, H2SO4, H3PO4.
          

  
          How statements become symbols
          
  
          Two rules run, in this order, and both remove things rather than add
     them. Neither can be switched off, because printing both halves of a
     pair is wrong rather than merely untidy.
          
  
          
    
    
          Signal word follows the statements that survive:
      Danger if any of them carries it, otherwise Warning.
          
  
          

  
          How strength changes a classification
          
  
          A dilute solution is often classified lower than the concentrated
     chemical, or not at all. Two tables can answer that, and they are not
     equal in authority.
          
  
          
    
          RuleWhen it is usedExample
          
    
          
      Published limits
      Where the substance has its own concentration limits. These are
          specific to the chemical and beat the generic table.
      Hydrochloric acid is corrosive at 25% and above, a skin and eye
          irritant from 10%, and below 10% carries neither.
    
          
    
          
      Generic cut-offs
      Everything else. Appendix B, Tables 15 and 16 of the national
          guide.
      A category 1 skin corrosive becomes an irritant between 1% and
          5%, and drops out below 1%.
    
          
  
          
  
          Physical hazards (flammability, oxidising) and environmental hazards
     are carried through unchanged, because the GHS
     requires the mixture itself to be tested for those rather than
     calculated. Keeping them is the conservative error.
          
  
          A label built from ingredients takes a different route again: each
     component is judged at its own percentage, then skin and eye
     corrosives are added up (section 3.6) and acute toxicity is combined
     through the ATEmix formula (section 3.5). A mixture is never offered a
     single strength, because one percentage cannot describe two components
     at two concentrations.
          

  
          Sizes: what is required, and what is only recommended
          
  
          
    There are no mandatory sizes for a workplace label.
    Safe Work Australia says so directly: sizes become mandatory only where
    the label carries ADG elements, and then the ADG Code's own table
    applies. The sizes this program recommends — 15 mm symbols
    and 2.5 mm text for a container of 500 mL or less, rising to
    100 mm and 7 mm above 25 kg or litres — are the
    Code of Practice reproducing ADG Table 5.2. Good practice, not a bar
    you are failing.
  
          
  
          Small containers are expressly allowed less. Where size prevents
     showing everything clearly, the regulations ask for as much as will
     fit, with the most significant hazards first — which is exactly
     what the fit does when it shortens statements to codes on a
     54 × 25 mm roll label. For a decanted container
     the minimum is the product identifier plus either a pictogram or a
     hazard statement.
          

  
          The law this answers to
          
  
          
    
          InstrumentWhat it governs here
          
    
          
      Model WHS Regulations
          
          Tasmania’s
          own version is linked below, and is the operative one here.          		
      Schedule 6 (the hazard classes Australia adopted),
          Schedule 9 (what a label must carry), Schedules 10
          and 11.
    
          
    
          
      Classifying hazardous chemicals
          — national guide (June 2023)
      The cut-off tables, the mixture rules, and the acute toxicity
          point estimates this program uses.
    
          
    
          
      Code of Practice: Labelling of
          workplace hazardous chemicals
      What goes on a label, and the recommended element sizes.
    
          
    
          
      Safe Work Australia —
          label information
      Small containers, and the statement that WHS label sizes are not
          mandatory.
    
          
    
          
      GHS Revision 7 (adoption)
      Statement wording, pictogram precedence, and the mixture tables
          the guide points to but does not reproduce.
    
          
    
          
      ADG Code
      Transport class and UN number; label sizes where ADG elements
          appear; the environmentally hazardous substance mark.
    
          
  
          

  
          Tasmania
          
  
          
    
          
      Work Health and Safety
          Regulations 2022 (Tas)
      The model regulations as they actually apply here. Chapter 7
          is hazardous chemicals.
    
          
    
          
      WorkSafe Tasmania — Acts
          and regulations
      The Work Health and Safety Act 2012 (Tas) and the regulator's own
          guidance.
    
          
    
          
      EPA Tasmania
      Disposal, spills to drains and waterways. None of this is WHS: it
          sits under the Environmental Management and Pollution Control Act
          1994.
    
          
    
          
      IChEMS
      The national environmental scheme, with its
          register of seven schedules.
          It restricts manufacture, import and use; it puts nothing on a
          label.
    
          
  
          

  
          
    Your department's own procedure. No public DECYP
    document on chemical management in schools could be found to cite, so
    nothing is claimed here. Their
    policy library is the place to
    look, and the local chemical management procedure, waste contractor and
    trade-waste conditions belong in this space. Where a school procedure is
    stricter than the law, the school procedure wins.
  
          

  
          Why environmental statements still appear
          
  
          Australia did not adopt the environmental hazard classes into the WHS
     Regulations, so a chemical that is only hazardous to the
     environment is not a hazardous chemical under those regulations at all.
     H400, H410 and the fish-and-tree symbol are therefore optional on a
     workplace label — optional, not prohibited, and they are kept
     here for three reasons: they are true, they are the clearest cue
     against tipping something down a sink, and they become
     mandatory in transport, where the ADG Code requires
     the environmentally hazardous substance mark on packages of UN 3077
     and 3082.
          

  
          What this does not do
          
  
          
    
          Replace an SDS
        It summarises; the SDS governs.
          
    
          Classify from test data
        It reads published classifications and applies published
            cut-offs. It cannot judge an untested mixture.
          
    
          Decide physical or environmental hazards of a mixture
        Those require the mixture itself to be tested. They are carried
            through unchanged from the ingredients.
          
    
          Cover transport paperwork
        It prints a class and UN number for reference. Manifests,
            placarding and emergency action codes are elsewhere.
          
    
          Know your stock
        Quantities, locations, expiry and disposal records are not held
            here.
          
  
          

  
          Every screen in this program will
     tell you where its answer came from if you open the panel beside it.
     Where it is unsure, it says so rather than guessing — a blank is
     a question, not a clearance.
          

  
          

          


          
  
  
          
    Storage notes file
    
          
      
          One note per chemical, kept apart from the labels
        because the note describes the chemical and the prep room, not the
        bottle. Twenty decants of nitric acid share one note. Export it to
        keep a copy, or to give the same notes to another prep room.
          
      
          
      
          
        
        
      
          
      
    
          
  
          

  
          
    Border colours — segregation groups
    
          
      
          The border says which cabinet a bottle goes back in.
        Red, yellow and blue come straight from the dangerous goods diamonds
        for classes 3, 5.1 and 4.3 so they do not fight that convention.
        Class 8 is one diamond covering both acids and bases, so it splits
        into the two hues nothing else in the DG set claims.
          
      
          
        
        
        
          Yellow is deliberately not used for acids — nitric
          acid and potassium permanganate wearing the same colour is the
          confusion this is meant to prevent.

    Moving labels around
    
          
      
          
        Build sheet lays every queued label onto the page —
        press it again at any time to put everything back. Then click a label
        to select it: drag it to move, drag the blue corner to resize, and
        remove it with the × in its corner or the
        Delete key. Dashed guides show where the stickers
        are on the chosen sheet.
      
          
      
          
        
        
          Drop a label near a sticker
          and it clicks into place. Turn this off to position freely, for
          printing on plain paper.
          
      
          
    
          
  
          

  
          
    When the text does not fit
    
          
      
          
        
      
          
      
          
        
          
          
          
        
          
        
          
          % of the preset size
        
          
      
          
      
          
        
      
          
      
          Order: AKA, properties, precautionary statements, PPE/first aid, storage notes. Name, formula, signal word, pictograms and class/UN are never dropped.
          
    
          
  
          

  
          
    Before you print onto label sheets
    
          
      
          In the browser's print dialog set
        Scale to 100% — not “Fit to page”,
        which shrinks everything and pushes the labels out of alignment
        — and Margins to None. Turn
        Background graphics on so the coloured borders print.
          
      
          Do a test print on plain paper first and hold it
        against a label sheet before using the real thing.

                Create a chemical mixture label
                
      
                
        
                For something made up in the prep room. Each
          ingredient is looked up, then the cut-offs decide what still counts
          at the strength you used. A mixture bought ready-made should
          be classified from its own safety data sheet instead — the
          supplier's classification is the one that governs it.

                Convert an SDS to a Label
                
      
                
        
                
          
          Drop the sheet here
          The classification is read out of it, the sheet
            itself is filed, and the Mini SDS takes its first-aid and storage
            wording from it afterwards.
          
          
        
                
        
                PDF, Word .docx, or plain text and HTML.
          Pictures cannot be read — a .jpg, a .png or a scanned PDF is a
          picture of words rather than words, and pulling text out of one needs
          OCR this page does not carry. Ask the supplier for the PDF, or copy
          the text and paste it under Search › Paste from HCIS.

                  What the border colours mean
                  
        
                  Every label is edged in the colour of the group it
          belongs to, so a shelf reads at a glance. Click a colour to change
          it — useful for matching tape or labels already on your
          cupboards.
